absd.short: An extra stamp duty, on top of BSD, whose rate depends on the buyers' residency status and how many residential properties they already own.
absd.formula: ABSD = ABSD rate for the buyer profile × higher of (price, market value)
absd.body:
ABSD is designed to moderate demand for additional homes and purchases by non-citizens. The rate is set by IRAS for each combination of residency status and number of residential properties owned. Singapore Citizens buying their first residential property pay none; Permanent Residents pay ABSD even on a first property, and rates rise steeply for second and later properties. Foreigners cannot buy HDB flats.

When joint buyers have different profiles, the highest applicable rate applies to the whole purchase. IRAS offers remission in some cases — for example, to certain married couples buying their first home together, or to owners who sell their previous flat within a set period.

Worked example: e.g. a couple who are both Permanent Residents buying a S$500,000 resale flat as their first home would pay ABSD at the Permanent Resident first-property rate on S$500,000, on top of BSD. This app looks up that rate from the current IRAS table.

Tip: Any share in a residential property, including an inherited one, can count towards the number of properties owned, so checking the household's profile against IRAS's rules early avoids surprises.

accrued-interest.short: The interest that CPF savings used for a flat would have earned in the Ordinary Account; it is refunded to CPF, with the principal, when the flat is sold.
accrued-interest.formula: Refund on sale = CPF principal used + accrued interest at the OA rate (compounded)
accrued-interest.body:
When CPF savings go into a home, they stop earning interest in the Ordinary Account. To protect retirement savings, CPF tracks the interest those savings would have earned — at the OA rate of at least {policy:proposed.cpf.oa.rate} a year, compounded — as accrued interest.

When the flat is sold, the proceeds first repay any outstanding loan, then refund the CPF principal used plus accrued interest into the owners' CPF accounts. The money remains the owners' own savings, but it goes back into CPF rather than to them as cash.

Worked example: e.g. S$100,000 of CPF used for a flat and left for 10 years at an illustrative 3%, compounded yearly for simplicity, grows to about S$134,000 to be refunded on sale.

Tip: If an HDB flat is sold at market value and the proceeds fall short of the full refund, owners generally do not have to top up the difference in cash. Owners can also make voluntary refunds to reduce the amount that builds up.

amortisation.short: The gradual paying-off of a loan through regular instalments, with the interest share of each payment shrinking and the principal share growing over time.
amortisation.formula: Interest this month = outstanding balance × annual rate ÷ 12; principal repaid = instalment − interest
amortisation.body:
An amortisation schedule lists every instalment over the life of the loan and splits each one into interest and principal. Interest is charged on the balance still owed, so in the early years most of the instalment is interest. As the balance falls, the interest portion shrinks and more of each payment reduces the debt.

This is why the outstanding loan falls slowly at first and faster towards the end. It also explains why a partial prepayment made early in the loan saves more interest than the same amount paid late.

Worked example: e.g. on a S$400,000 loan at an illustrative 3.2%, the first month's interest is about S$1,070 (S$400,000 × 3.2% ÷ 12). With an instalment of about S$2,260, only about S$1,190 goes to principal that month.

Tip: The balance left after some years matters when thinking about selling or refinancing, because it has to be repaid from the sale proceeds or the new loan.

bank-loan.short: A home loan from a bank or financial institution, priced off market rates, with an LTV of up to {policy:loan.bank.ltv} and both MSR and TDSR checks.
bank-loan.body:
HDB flat buyers can borrow from a bank instead of HDB. Bank loans are not subject to HDB's income ceiling, and their rates follow the market, so they can be lower or higher than the HDB rate at different times.

MAS sets the rules. A first housing loan can be up to {policy:loan.bank.ltv} of the lower of price and valuation (or {policy:loan.bank.ltv.lower_tier} if the tenure or age limits are exceeded), and the tenure on an HDB flat is capped at {policy:tenure.bank.hdb_flat.max} years. At least {policy:downpayment.bank.cash_min} of the price must be paid in cash. The loan must pass both MSR ({policy:ratio.msr.cap}) and TDSR ({policy:ratio.tdsr.cap}), tested at {policy:rate.floor.bank} or the actual rate if higher.

Worked example: e.g. a S$500,000 flat bought with a bank loan needs a cash portion in the downpayment, while the same flat with an HDB loan could be paid for entirely from CPF and the loan.

Tip: Moving from an HDB loan to a bank loan later is possible, but moving from a bank loan back to an HDB loan is not.

bridging-loan.short: A short bank loan that pays the cash part of your next home's downpayment until the money from selling your current home comes in.
bridging-loan.body:
If you buy the next home before the sale of your current one completes, the downpayment is due before the sale money arrives. A bridging loan from a bank covers that gap for a short time and is repaid from the sale proceeds.

Bridging loans come from banks, not HDB. They charge interest for the time you use them, and the bank looks at your income and at the sale you have already agreed.

Tip: Compare the cost of a bridging loan with the other ways to bridge the gap — a contra (both completions together) or an extension of stay — before you commit. This app does not add a bridging loan to its numbers.

brs.short: The lowest of the three CPF retirement sums; an owner of a property with enough lease left can pledge it and set aside only the BRS in the Retirement Account at age {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation}.
brs.body:
The sums depend on the year you turn {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation} and stay fixed for you from then. By that year:

{policy:cpf.retirement_sums}

Setting aside only the BRS (with a property pledge) frees the savings above it, but the CPF LIFE payout for life is lower than with the FRS.

Tip: in Plan → CPF & retirement each buyer's card ticks the BRS and FRS when the projected Retirement Account reaches them.

bsd.short: A tax on buying property, charged at tiered rates on the higher of the price or market value, and payable on every purchase.
bsd.formula: BSD = sum over bands of (portion of value in band × band rate)
bsd.body:
BSD applies to every property purchase in Singapore, including HDB resale flats. It is calculated on the higher of the purchase price and the market value, using progressive bands: a low rate on the first slice of value and higher rates on each further slice, as set out in the IRAS rate table. The result is rounded down to the nearest dollar.

BSD must be paid within {policy:proposed.stamp.duty.payment_days} days of signing the purchase document. It can be paid in cash or with CPF Ordinary Account savings, subject to CPF rules.

Worked example: e.g. for a S$600,000 flat, the first band of value is taxed at the lowest rate, the next band at a higher rate, and so on until the full S$600,000 is covered. This app adds up the bands from the current IRAS table.

Tip: Because the rates rise band by band, BSD grows faster than the price, so a higher-priced flat carries a proportionally larger duty.

chg.short: A fixed grant for first-timer families buying a resale flat, larger for flats of up to four rooms than for five-room and bigger flats.
chg.body:
Often called the Family Grant, this grant helps first-timer families buy a flat on the resale market. Unlike the EHG it is not tiered by income: eligible households receive a fixed amount set by flat size — a higher amount for two- to four-room flats, a lower one for five-room and larger flats — provided household income does not exceed {policy:eligibility.income_ceiling.family} a month.

The grant is credited to the buyers' CPF accounts and used towards the purchase. At least one buyer must be a Singapore Citizen. Lower amounts apply when the other buyer is a Permanent Resident, when only one buyer is a first-timer, and to singles.

Worked example: e.g. a first-timer couple buying a four-room resale flat could combine this grant with the EHG (if their income qualifies) and the Proximity Housing Grant, reducing the loan or downpayment they need.

Tip: Because grants are paid into CPF, they count as CPF used for the flat and are refunded to CPF with accrued interest when it is sold.

contra.short: Selling your current home and buying the next one so that both complete on the same day, letting the money from the sale pay for part of the purchase.
contra.body:
In a contra, the sale of the home you own and the purchase of the next one are completed together. The cash from the sale (after your loan and the CPF refund) goes straight into the purchase, so you do not need that cash up front.

It only works when both dates line up. An HDB resale completes within about {policy:sellbuy.resale.completion_days} days of HDB accepting the resale application, so the two transactions are timed together.

If the dates cannot line up, the usual ways around it are to stay on in the sold flat for a while (extension of stay) or to borrow the gap for a short time (bridging loan).

Tip: Ask HDB and your lawyer early whether your sale and purchase can be completed together. The Plan tab shows the cash and CPF that come back from the sale.

cov.short: The amount by which an agreed resale price exceeds HDB's valuation; it cannot be covered by a loan or CPF and must be paid in cash.
cov.formula: COV = max(0, agreed price − HDB valuation)
cov.body:
In an HDB resale, buyer and seller agree a price, then HDB assesses the flat's value. The loan and CPF usage are based on the lower of the two. If the price is higher, the difference is Cash Over Valuation, and it has to be paid in cash.

COV is not a fee or a tax; it is part of the price that cannot be borrowed against. It tends to appear when demand is strong and fade when the market cools.

Worked example: e.g. agreed price S$650,000, valuation S$630,000: COV is S$20,000 in cash. The loan is capped at {policy:loan.hdb.ltv} (HDB loan) or {policy:loan.bank.ltv} (bank loan) of S$630,000, not of the price.

Tip: The valuation is only known after the Option to Purchase is granted, so many buyers keep a cash buffer for possible COV. This app's recent-sales benchmark gives a sense of whether an asking price sits above nearby transactions.

cpf-housing.short: CPF Ordinary Account savings can pay the downpayment, stamp duty, legal fees and instalments, within limits linked to the flat's value and remaining lease.
cpf-housing.body:
CPF lets members put their Ordinary Account savings towards a home: the downpayment (all of it, with an HDB loan), Buyer's Stamp Duty, legal fees and the monthly instalments afterwards.

Two sets of limits shape how much can be used. First, the Valuation Limit and Withdrawal Limit tie CPF usage to the lower of price and valuation. Second, the lease rule: full use is allowed only if the remaining lease covers the youngest buyer to age {policy:cpf.lease.cover_to_age}; otherwise the usable amount is pro-rated, and CPF cannot be used at all if the remaining lease is below {policy:cpf.lease.min_years} years. Members taking an HDB loan may keep up to {policy:proposed.cpf.oa.retain_with_hdb_loan} in their OA.

Worked example: e.g. a youngest buyer aged 35 and a flat with 55 years of lease left: the check is whether 35 + 55 reaches {policy:cpf.lease.cover_to_age}. If it falls short, CPF usage is pro-rated.

Tip: Using more CPF lowers the cash needed, but all CPF used is refunded with accrued interest when the flat is sold.

cpf-life.short: The national annuity that turns your CPF Retirement Account savings into a monthly payout for as long as you live, starting from age {policy:cpf.age.life_payout}.
cpf-life.body:
CPF LIFE (Lifelong Income For the Elderly) uses the savings in your Retirement Account (RA) to pay you every month from age {policy:cpf.age.life_payout}, for life. The more you have in the RA when you turn {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation}, the larger the payout — so CPF used for a home earlier, which is not there to form the RA, means a smaller payout later.

The app's CPF LIFE figure is approximate: it scales CPF's published examples to your projected RA. The plan you choose, top-ups and starting the payout later change the amount and are not modelled. CPF's own planner gives your actual estimate.

Tip: Plan → CPF & retirement shows the estimate with and without the flat you picked, side by side.

cpf-oa.short: The CPF account most used for housing, funded by monthly employee and employer contributions and earning at least {policy:proposed.cpf.oa.rate} a year.
cpf-oa.body:
Working Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents contribute part of their monthly wages to CPF, and their employers add more. A large share flows into the Ordinary Account, the main source of CPF money for buying a home.

OA savings can pay for the downpayment, stamp duty, legal fees and monthly instalments, within the limits set by CPF. The OA earns at least {policy:proposed.cpf.oa.rate} a year, and the HDB concessionary loan rate ({policy:rate.hdb.concessionary}) is pegged just above the OA rate.

Worked example: e.g. a couple with S$80,000 combined in their OAs could put it towards the downpayment and fees, then pay part of the instalment from their ongoing monthly contributions.

Tip: Every dollar of OA used for housing stops earning CPF interest and must be returned with accrued interest when the flat is sold, so using CPF trades off against retirement savings.

downpayment.short: The part of the purchase price not covered by the loan, paid from CPF and/or cash; its size and cash portion depend on the loan type.
downpayment.body:
The downpayment is the buyer's own contribution to the price. With an HDB loan of up to {policy:loan.hdb.ltv}, the remainder can be paid with CPF Ordinary Account savings, cash, or both. With a bank loan of up to {policy:loan.bank.ltv}, at least {policy:downpayment.bank.cash_min} of the price must be paid in cash, and the rest of the downpayment can come from CPF.

Because the loan is based on the lower of price and valuation, any Cash Over Valuation is added on top of the normal downpayment and must be paid in cash.

Worked example: e.g. a S$600,000 flat valued at S$600,000: the downpayment is the price minus the loan. If the agreed price were S$620,000 with the same valuation, the extra S$20,000 is COV, payable in cash on top.

Tip: Housing grants are credited to CPF and go towards the purchase, so the grant amount in the HFE letter directly reduces what the household has to find.

ehg.short: An income-tiered grant for first-timer households buying a new or resale flat — the lower the household income, the larger the grant.
ehg.body:
The EHG supports first-time buyers with lower and middle incomes. The amount depends on the household's average gross monthly income over the twelve months before applying: HDB's table sets out income bands, with the largest grant for the lowest band and smaller amounts as income rises, up to an income ceiling above which no EHG is given. Singles have their own, smaller table. At least one buyer must have been working continuously in that period.

The grant is credited to the buyers' CPF Ordinary Accounts and must go towards the flat, reducing the downpayment or loan. For resale flats it can be combined with the CPF Housing Grant and the Proximity Housing Grant. The full amount needs the remaining lease to cover the youngest buyer to age {policy:cpf.lease.cover_to_age}; otherwise it is pro-rated.

Worked example: e.g. a first-timer couple averaging S$6,000 a month would find their tier in HDB's EHG table; a couple earning more would receive a smaller amount, or none.

Tip: The HFE letter states the exact EHG amount for the household.

extension-of-stay.short: An arrangement where the buyer of your HDB flat lets you keep living there for a short time after the sale completes, up to {policy:sellbuy.extension_of_stay.max_months} months.
extension-of-stay.body:
When you sell first and your next home is not ready yet, you can ask for a temporary extension of stay: you stay on in the flat you sold for up to {policy:sellbuy.extension_of_stay.max_months} months after the resale completes, with no further extension.

The buyer must agree, and it is only for sellers who have already committed to buy a completed home (an exercised Option to Purchase or a signed sale agreement). You receive the sale money on completion, so the next purchase can use it, and you avoid moving twice.

Tip: Agree the length and terms with the buyer early, before you grant the Option to Purchase.

fair-value.term: Recent sales benchmark (fair value in this app)
fair-value.short: This app's reference price for a flat, built from recent resale transactions of similar flats in the same block or town — a reference point, not a valuation.
fair-value.formula: Benchmark price = recent comparable $psf × flat's floor area
fair-value.body:
The app compares an asking price with recent sales of similar flats: the same flat type, in the same block where there are enough sales, otherwise in the same town. It expresses the benchmark as a price per square foot and applies it to the flat's floor area.

The benchmark summarises past transactions, so it lags the market and cannot see a flat's condition, view, renovation or exact position. It is not HDB's valuation, which is only known after the Option to Purchase, and it is not a prediction.

Worked example: e.g. if similar flats in the block recently sold at about S$600 psf and a 1,000 sq ft flat is listed at S$650,000, the asking price is about S$50,000 above the benchmark — a gap that could turn into COV if HDB's valuation is close to recent sales.

Tip: A large gap in either direction is a prompt to look more closely at the listing, not a verdict on it.

first-timer.short: A buyer who has never bought a subsidised flat or received a CPF housing grant — the status that unlocks the largest housing grants.
first-timer.body:
HDB classifies buyers by their housing history. A first-timer has not previously enjoyed a housing subsidy — for example, has not bought a new flat from HDB or a resale flat with a CPF housing grant. Owning private property also affects eligibility for grants.

A couple are first-timers when both partners are. If one has already received a subsidy, the household is treated as "first-timer and second-timer", which has its own grant amounts.

This matters for affordability. First-timer families can receive the CPF Housing Grant and the Enhanced CPF Housing Grant on a resale flat, while second-timer households are mainly limited to the Proximity Housing Grant.

Worked example: e.g. a couple where one partner earlier bought a new flat from HDB with their parents would generally not count as a full first-timer household.

Tip: The HFE letter confirms each buyer's status, which removes the guesswork.

fixed-vs-floating.short: A fixed rate stays the same for an agreed period; a floating rate moves with a benchmark such as SORA, so the instalment can rise or fall.
fixed-vs-floating.body:
Bank home loans come in two broad types. Fixed-rate packages hold the interest rate for a set period, often the first few years, giving predictable instalments. Floating-rate packages are pegged to a benchmark — usually SORA — plus a spread, so the instalment changes when the benchmark moves. When a fixed period ends, the rate typically reverts to a floating rate.

The HDB concessionary loan is a third kind. Its rate, currently {policy:rate.hdb.concessionary}, is reviewed quarterly in line with the CPF Ordinary Account rate, so it can change, but historically it has moved very little.

Worked example: e.g. on a S$400,000 loan over 20 years, a rate move from 3.2% to 4.2% lifts the instalment from about S$2,260 to about S$2,470. A floating-rate borrower feels this at the next reset; a fixed-rate borrower only when the fixed period ends.

Tip: Many bank packages have a lock-in period with a penalty for early repayment or refinancing, so those terms are part of comparing loans, not just the headline rate.

flexi.short: A small HDB flat for seniors and singles; buyers aged {policy:seniors.flexi.min_age} or older choose a short lease that covers the youngest owner to at least age {policy:seniors.flexi.cover_to_age}.
flexi.body:
Two-room Flexi flats are the smallest new HDB flats. Seniors aged {policy:seniors.flexi.min_age} or older can buy one on a short lease, chosen in steps, as long as it covers the youngest owner and spouse to at least age {policy:seniors.flexi.cover_to_age}. A shorter lease costs less, so more of the sale money from a larger flat can go to retirement. Household income must be within {policy:seniors.flexi.income_ceiling} a month.

Singles buying a new flat on their own are also offered two-room Flexi flats. Right-sizing to one can add to the Silver Housing Bonus.

Tip: The Options card in Plan lists the short-lease two-room Flexi as one of the paths, with whether you are eligible.

floor-rate.short: A minimum interest rate lenders use when checking affordability — {policy:rate.floor.hdb} for HDB loans and {policy:rate.floor.bank} for bank loans — even if the actual rate is lower.
floor-rate.formula: Assessment rate = max(actual rate, floor rate)
floor-rate.body:
When HDB or a bank works out how much it can lend, it does not plug today's interest rate into the MSR and TDSR checks. It uses the higher of the actual rate and a floor rate: {policy:rate.floor.hdb} for an HDB loan, and {policy:rate.floor.bank} for a bank loan on residential property.

The floor exists so that borrowers can still cope if rates rise. Because it is often above the rate actually charged — the HDB concessionary rate is currently {policy:rate.hdb.concessionary} — the maximum loan is smaller than a calculation at the real rate would suggest.

Worked example: e.g. a S$400,000 loan over 20 years. The instalment used for the MSR check is computed at the floor rate, so it is higher than the instalment the borrower will actually pay. It is that floor-rate instalment that must fit within {policy:ratio.msr.cap} of income.

Tip: The gap between the floor-rate instalment and the actual instalment is a built-in safety margin; comparing the two shows how much room the household has if rates go up.

frs.short: The CPF retirement sum your Retirement Account is filled up to at age {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation}, unless you pledge a property; higher than the Basic Retirement Sum, and fixed by the year you turn {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation}.
frs.body:
At {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation}, savings from the Special and Ordinary Accounts move into the Retirement Account until the FRS is reached; savings above it stay available. The Enhanced Retirement Sum is {policy:cpf.retirement_sums.ers_multiple} times the FRS — the most you may put in for a higher payout.

By the year you turn {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation}:

{policy:cpf.retirement_sums}

Tip: CPF used for a flat is not there to form the RA. Plan → CPF & retirement shows whether each buyer reaches the FRS with and without the flat you picked.

future-value.short: A per-driver scorecard of the signals that have tended to move HDB resale values — lease runway, momentum against the market, relative value, catalysts, supply, rental yield, liquidity and scarcity — each scored on its own, with no overall number.
future-value.body:
The comparison table's future-value section looks at eight things that have historically been linked with how a resale flat's value holds up: how much lease will be left when you might sell, how the town's prices moved against HDB's Resale Price Index, whether the flat is priced below or above similar-lease sales, new MRT stations and major projects nearby, how much fresh supply (new BTO flats and flats reaching their MOP) is coming, the rental yield, how often flats in the block change hands, and how rare the flat type is in the town.

Each driver gets a score from 1 to 5 from fixed cut-offs, with a one-line reason. There is deliberately no overall score: the drivers pull in different directions, and how much each matters depends on your plans.

Worked example: e.g. a flat may score well on rental yield and liquidity but poorly on lease runway — a reminder to weigh the lease more if you plan to sell in ten years.

Tip: None of these drivers predicts prices. Master Plan zoning is not a committed project, rents are declared rents, and past momentum is not a guide to future returns.

hdb-loan.short: A housing loan from HDB for eligible households, at a rate pegged slightly above the CPF Ordinary Account rate — currently {policy:rate.hdb.concessionary} a year.
hdb-loan.body:
HDB lends to eligible buyers with at least one Singapore Citizen in the household. The interest rate is pegged a small margin above the CPF Ordinary Account rate and reviewed quarterly; it is currently {policy:rate.hdb.concessionary}. It has historically been very stable, though not always the cheapest option.

Key limits: the loan is up to {policy:loan.hdb.ltv} of the lower of price and valuation; the tenure is at most {policy:tenure.hdb.max} years; the instalment must pass the MSR cap of {policy:ratio.msr.cap} at the {policy:rate.floor.hdb} floor rate; and family household income must not exceed {policy:eligibility.income_ceiling.family} a month. Ordinary Account savings are generally used first, though buyers may keep up to {policy:proposed.cpf.oa.retain_with_hdb_loan} in the account.

Worked example: e.g. for a S$500,000 flat, the downpayment under an HDB loan can be paid entirely from CPF, whereas a bank loan needs part of it in cash.

Tip: A valid HFE letter confirming loan eligibility is needed before a seller can grant the Option to Purchase.

hfe.short: A letter from HDB, applied for before house-hunting, that states whether a household can buy a flat, which grants it qualifies for and how much HDB will lend.
hfe.body:
The HFE letter brings three checks into one application: eligibility to buy an HDB flat, eligibility for CPF housing grants (and the amounts), and eligibility for an HDB housing loan, including the maximum loan. It is based on the household's details and income at the time of application.

For resale buyers who plan to take an HDB loan, a valid HFE letter is required before the seller can grant the Option to Purchase. The letter is valid for {policy:proposed.hfe.validity_months} months.

Worked example: e.g. a couple's letter states a maximum HDB loan of S$450,000 and grants of S$50,000. Added to their CPF savings and cash, this gives a realistic ceiling for the flats they shortlist.

Tip: A new job, a change in income or a change in who is in the household can alter the outcome, so the letter reflects a point in time rather than a permanent entitlement.

hps.short: A CPF-run mortgage-reducing insurance that pays off an insured member's share of the HDB flat loan if they die or suffer terminal illness or total permanent disability.
hps.body:
HPS protects a household from losing its HDB flat if a borrower can no longer pay. If an insured member dies, is diagnosed with a terminal illness or becomes totally and permanently disabled, CPF settles their insured share of the outstanding loan directly with HDB or the bank.

It is required for members using CPF savings to pay the monthly instalments on an HDB flat. Cover lasts until the member reaches age {policy:proposed.hps.cover_to_age} or the loan is paid off, whichever comes first. Premiums are deducted yearly from the Ordinary Account and depend on the loan amount, tenure and age.

Worked example: e.g. a couple who pay 60% and 40% of the instalment would typically take shares of cover at least in those proportions, adding up to at least 100% of the loan.

Tip: Because HPS is mortgage-reducing, the sum insured falls as the loan is repaid; it covers the home loan only, not other living costs.

income-ceiling.short: The maximum average gross monthly household income allowed to qualify for an HDB loan or a housing grant; each scheme sets its own ceiling.
income-ceiling.formula: Average gross monthly household income = total gross income over the past 12 months ÷ 12
income-ceiling.body:
HDB uses household income to target its help. For families, both the HDB concessionary loan and the CPF Housing Grant for resale flats require an average gross monthly household income of no more than {policy:eligibility.income_ceiling.family}; a single buying alone faces a ceiling of {policy:eligibility.income_ceiling.single}. The Enhanced CPF Housing Grant has its own, lower ceiling and is tiered by income below it.

Income is usually averaged over the twelve months before the application and covers the gross income of all buyers and, in some cases, other listed occupiers.

Exceeding a ceiling does not stop a household from buying a resale flat; it means borrowing from a bank instead of HDB, or missing out on a grant.

Worked example: e.g. a household earning S$15,000 a month is compared against each ceiling separately — it can be above one and below another.

instalment.short: The fixed monthly repayment on a home loan, covering that month's interest plus part of the principal.
instalment.formula: Instalment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where P = loan, r = annual rate ÷ 12, n = tenure in months
instalment.body:
The instalment is what the borrower pays each month. For a standard home loan it stays the same as long as the interest rate stays the same. Early on most of it is interest; over time more of it goes to reducing the principal.

Three things set the instalment: the loan amount, the interest rate and the tenure. A bigger loan or a higher rate increases it; a longer tenure reduces it.

For affordability checks, lenders compute the instalment at the floor rate — {policy:rate.floor.hdb} for HDB loans, {policy:rate.floor.bank} for bank loans — whenever that is higher than the actual rate, and compare it with the MSR cap of {policy:ratio.msr.cap} of income.

Worked example: e.g. a S$400,000 loan over 20 years at an illustrative 3.2% costs about S$2,260 a month. At an illustrative 4.2%, the same loan costs about S$2,470.

Tip: A rate change of around one percentage point moves the instalment by a couple of hundred dollars a month on a loan of this size, which is why rate assumptions matter.

intent-to-sell.short: The first step to sell an HDB flat — you register it on the HDB Flat Portal at least {policy:sellbuy.intent_to_sell.days_before_otp} days before you grant an Option to Purchase.
intent-to-sell.body:
Before selling, you register an Intent to Sell on the HDB Flat Portal, and HDB checks that you are eligible to sell — for example, that the Minimum Occupation Period is met.

The Intent to Sell must be valid and registered at least {policy:sellbuy.intent_to_sell.days_before_otp} days before you grant an Option to Purchase to a buyer. Use that time to get your CPF statement (CPF used and accrued interest) and to plan where you will live next.

Tip: If you plan to sell and buy, register early so the sale and the next purchase can be timed together.

lbs.short: An HDB scheme for older owners: sell the tail end of your flat's lease to HDB, keep living in the flat, and use the proceeds to top up your CPF Retirement Account for a larger CPF LIFE payout. Every owner must be at least {policy:seniors.lbs.min_age}.
lbs.body:
With the Lease Buyback Scheme you keep a shorter lease — chosen by the age of the youngest owner, up to {policy:seniors.lbs.retain_max} years — and HDB buys the rest of the lease from you. You stay in the same flat; nothing changes day to day.

The money goes first into each owner's Retirement Account (RA), up to the amount HDB requires, and from there into CPF LIFE, which pays out monthly for life. After the required top-ups, up to {policy:seniors.lbs.cash_retention} of what is left (all owners together) is paid in cash; above that, each owner is first topped up towards the Full Retirement Sum and the rest is paid in cash too. Household income must be within {policy:seniors.lbs.income_ceiling} a month.

Tip: the app does not estimate LBS proceeds — HDB works them out from a valuation of your flat. The Options card in Plan shows whether the scheme may be open to you; HDB's own estimator gives the figures.

lease-decay.short: The tendency of a leasehold flat's value to fall as its remaining lease shortens, slowly at first and faster as the end of the lease approaches.
lease-decay.body:
Because an HDB flat returns to HDB at the end of its lease, its value must eventually fall towards zero. Lease decay describes that path. While a lot of lease remains, prices are driven mostly by location, size and the wider market; the effect of a short lease becomes more visible as fewer decades remain.

Financing rules can amplify the effect. Buyers of short-lease flats may face pro-rated CPF use and HDB loans if the lease does not cover them to age {policy:cpf.lease.cover_to_age}, which narrows the pool of buyers who can afford those flats.

Worked example: e.g. two similar four-room flats in the same town, one with 90 years left and one with 55 years left, may trade at quite different prices per square foot despite being the same size.

Tip: Lease decay in past transactions is an observed pattern, not a rule; future prices also depend on policy and demand.

lease-to-95.short: CPF savings and the HDB loan can be used in full only if the remaining lease covers the youngest buyer to age {policy:cpf.lease.cover_to_age}; otherwise both are pro-rated.
lease-to-95.formula: Full use if youngest buyer's age + remaining lease ≥ cover-to age
lease-to-95.body:
This rule links how much a buyer can borrow from HDB and use from CPF to whether the flat will last them a lifetime. The test is simple: add the youngest buyer's age to the flat's remaining lease. If the total reaches {policy:cpf.lease.cover_to_age}, CPF savings can be used up to the Valuation Limit and the HDB loan can go up to the full {policy:loan.hdb.ltv}.

If the total falls short, the usable CPF amount and the HDB loan limit are pro-rated down, so more of the price must be paid in cash. If the remaining lease is below {policy:cpf.lease.min_years} years, CPF savings cannot be used at all.

Worked example: e.g. youngest buyer aged 30 and a flat with 60 years left: 30 + 60 = 90, which is compared against {policy:cpf.lease.cover_to_age}. The same buyer and a flat with 70 years left gives 100.

Tip: The rule matters most for older flats and older buyers; checking it before the Option to Purchase avoids discovering a cash shortfall later.

lease.short: HDB flats are sold on leasehold — a lease of {policy:lease.term.years} years from the lease commencement date — after which the flat returns to HDB.
lease.formula: Remaining lease = lease term − years since lease commencement
lease.body:
Buying an HDB flat means buying the right to live in it for what is left of a {policy:lease.term.years}-year lease, not owning the land outright. The lease starts from the block's lease commencement date, not from when the current owner bought it.

A resale buyer takes over whatever is left of the lease. When the lease runs out, the flat returns to HDB and the owner receives nothing for it. This is why lease length matters for value, for financing and for CPF rules.

Worked example: e.g. a flat whose lease began 40 years ago has {policy:lease.term.years} minus 40 years left.

Tip: The lease commencement date is published with HDB's resale transaction data; it is not the same as the year the flat was last sold.

legal-fees.short: Fees paid to HDB or a law firm for handling the legal transfer of the flat and the mortgage documents.
legal-fees.body:
Buying a flat involves legal work: checking the title, preparing the transfer, registering the mortgage and handling stamp duty. In an HDB resale, buyers may appoint HDB to act for them or engage a private law firm; buyers with a bank loan commonly use a firm that the bank accepts.

HDB's conveyancing fees follow published rules and scale with the price, with extra charges for items such as stamp, registration and survey fees. Each side pays its own legal costs. CPF Ordinary Account savings can generally be used for legal fees on the purchase.

Worked example: e.g. on a S$600,000 flat, conveyancing and related fees typically come to a few thousand dollars — small relative to the price, but part of the money needed at completion.

Tip: HDB provides an online estimator for its conveyancing fees, which helps complete the upfront-cost picture before committing.

ltv.short: The maximum loan as a share of the lower of the flat's price and valuation — {policy:loan.hdb.ltv} for HDB loans and {policy:loan.bank.ltv} for a first bank loan.
ltv.formula: Max loan = LTV × lower of (price, valuation)
ltv.body:
LTV sets how much of the purchase can be borrowed. It is applied to the lower of the agreed price and HDB's valuation, so any amount paid above valuation is never financed.

For an HDB loan the limit is {policy:loan.hdb.ltv}, pro-rated downwards if the remaining lease does not cover the youngest buyer to age {policy:cpf.lease.cover_to_age}. For a first bank loan it is {policy:loan.bank.ltv}, falling to {policy:loan.bank.ltv.lower_tier} if the tenure on an HDB flat is longer than {policy:loan.bank.hdb_flat.full_ltv_max_tenure} years or the loan runs past age {policy:tenure.age_cap}.

Worked example: e.g. a flat priced at S$600,000 that is valued at S$580,000. The loan is calculated on S$580,000, and the buyer funds the rest — including the S$20,000 gap — from CPF and cash.

Tip: LTV is a ceiling, not a target. Borrowing less lowers the instalment and the total interest, but uses more savings upfront.

mop.short: The period, generally {policy:proposed.mop.years} years, during which owners must physically live in their flat before they can sell it on the open market.
mop.body:
The MOP keeps HDB flats for owner-occupation rather than short-term trading. Owners must physically live in the flat for the MOP — generally {policy:proposed.mop.years} years for resale flats — before they can sell it, rent out the whole flat or buy a private property.

The MOP is counted from the date the owners take possession of the flat. Periods when the whole flat is rented out do not count. Some newer flat types carry a longer MOP.

Worked example: e.g. a couple who complete a resale purchase this year can sell no earlier than {policy:proposed.mop.years} years after that date.

Tip: The MOP also matters when buying — a seller can only grant an Option to Purchase once they have met their own MOP.

msr.short: The share of gross monthly household income that goes to home-loan instalments; for HDB flats it may not exceed {policy:ratio.msr.cap}.
msr.formula: MSR = monthly instalment ÷ gross monthly household income
msr.body:
MSR measures how much of a household's gross monthly income is committed to the mortgage on the flat. For HDB flats the cap is {policy:ratio.msr.cap}, and it applies whether the loan comes from HDB or from a bank.

Lenders do not test MSR at the rate the borrower will actually pay. The instalment is worked out at the higher of the actual rate and a floor rate: {policy:rate.floor.hdb} for an HDB loan, or {policy:rate.floor.bank} for a bank loan. This builds in a buffer in case rates rise.

Worked example: e.g. a couple earning S$8,000 a month combined. Their instalment, computed at the floor rate, may be at most {policy:ratio.msr.cap} of S$8,000. That ceiling on the instalment, together with the tenure, sets the largest loan they can take.

Tip: MSR uses gross income, before CPF contributions, while the instalment is paid from CPF and take-home pay. Comparing the instalment with take-home pay as well gives a fuller picture of how comfortable it is.

ncq.short: A cap on how many flats in each HDB block and neighbourhood may be rented out whole to non-Malaysian non-citizens — it decides whether a landlord can rent the flat to you.
ncq.body:
When a whole HDB flat is rented out, HDB counts the tenants who are not Singapore Citizens or Malaysians. Each block and each neighbourhood has a cap on the share of flats rented to them; once a block reaches its cap, an owner there cannot rent the whole flat to another such tenant until the count falls.

The quota is about the landlord's block, not about you. A Permanent Resident or a foreigner looking for a whole flat should ask the landlord whether the block is under the quota before paying a deposit — HDB has an online check by block. Renting a room is not limited by this quota.

Tenancies for non-citizens are also approved for a limited period at a time, so a long stay means renewing with HDB.

Tip: Rent & Buy → "What your household can do" lists the renting rules that apply to your household.

option-fee.term: Option to Purchase (OTP) and option fee
option-fee.short: The OTP is the seller's offer to sell at an agreed price; the buyer pays an option fee to receive it and an exercise fee to take it up.
option-fee.formula: Option fee + exercise fee ≤ HDB cap; both form part of the price
option-fee.body:
In an HDB resale, the seller grants the buyer an Option to Purchase using HDB's standard form. To receive it, the buyer pays an option fee of up to {policy:proposed.resale.option_fee.max}. The buyer then has {policy:proposed.resale.otp.exercise_days} days to decide; exercising the option requires an exercise fee, with the two fees together capped at {policy:fees.option_exercise.max}.

Both fees are negotiable within those caps, form part of the resale price and must be paid in cash — CPF savings cannot be used for them. If the buyer does not exercise the option in time, the option fee goes to the seller.

Worked example: e.g. a buyer pays a S$500 option fee. If they exercise the option, it counts towards the price; if they let it lapse, the S$500 is lost.

Tip: Order matters — a buyer taking an HDB loan needs a valid HFE letter before the OTP is granted, and the Request for Value comes after it, so the valuation is not yet known when the option fee is paid.

phg.short: A grant for buyers of resale flats who will live with their parents or married child, or within {policy:grant.phg.near_km} km of them.
phg.body:
The PHG encourages families to live close together for mutual care and support. It applies to resale flats and is open to first-timers and second-timers alike, with no income ceiling, but each household can receive it only once.

There are two tiers: a larger amount to live together with parents or a married child in the same flat, and a smaller amount to live near them — within {policy:grant.phg.near_km} km. Singles have their own, smaller amounts.

Worked example: e.g. a couple comparing a flat within the distance limit of a parent's home with a similar flat further away would find the PHG narrows the price gap between the two.

Tip: The distance is measured between the two flats' addresses under HDB's rules, so a flat that looks close on a map may still fall outside the limit.

pr.short: A non-citizen with permanent residence. PR households can buy a resale HDB flat after holding PR for some years, but not a new flat from HDB, and pay ABSD on a home.
pr.body:
The rules for Permanent Residents differ from those for citizens in four ways that matter for a home:

  • New flats: a household of Permanent Residents with no citizen cannot buy a new flat from HDB.
  • Resale flats: a PR household can buy a resale flat once every PR in it has held PR for the minimum period HDB sets. Non-Malaysian PR households must also fit the block and neighbourhood SPR quota.
  • Loans and grants: an HDB loan needs at least one Singapore Citizen buyer, so PR-only households borrow from a bank. CPF housing grants also need a citizen buyer.
  • Stamp duty: Permanent Residents pay Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty, from their first home.

A single PR cannot buy an HDB flat at all; renting, a resale EC or a private home are the routes until citizenship.

Tip: Set each buyer's residency in Your household — the app then shows only the paths and loans that apply.

property-tax.short: An annual tax on property based on its Annual Value; owner-occupied HDB flats enjoy lower progressive rates, starting at zero for the lowest band.
property-tax.formula: Property tax = Annual Value taxed through the owner-occupier rate bands
property-tax.body:
IRAS levies property tax every year on all properties, based on the Annual Value — the estimated yearly rent the property could fetch, excluding furniture. For an HDB flat that the owner lives in, concessionary owner-occupier rates apply: the lowest band of Annual Value is taxed at zero and higher bands at progressively higher rates.

Because HDB flats generally have modest Annual Values, many owner-occupiers pay little property tax, and the Government sometimes grants one-off rebates. If the whole flat is rented out, the owner-occupier rates stop applying and higher non-owner-occupier rates take over.

Worked example: e.g. a flat with an Annual Value of S$20,000 is taxed at zero on the lowest band and at the owner-occupier rates only on the portion above it.

Tip: The owner-occupier rates apply to only one property — the one the owner actually lives in.

psf.short: The transacted price of a resale flat, and that price divided by floor area in square feet — a way to compare flats of different sizes.
psf.body:
Every completed HDB resale transaction is published with its price, flat type, floor area, storey range and lease commencement date. The headline price is what buyer and seller agreed, including any Cash Over Valuation.

Price per square foot (psf) adjusts for size. HDB records floor area in square metres, so the area is converted to square feet first. A bigger flat usually costs more in total but often less per square foot.

Worked example: e.g. a S$550,000 flat of 92 square metres (about 990 sq ft) works out to about S$555 psf; a S$480,000 flat of 68 square metres (about 732 sq ft) is about S$656 psf.

Tip: Psf is most meaningful when comparing flats with similar remaining lease, location and flat type; storey and condition also move prices.

ra.short: The CPF account created when you turn {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation}, from your Special Account and then your Ordinary Account, up to the Full Retirement Sum; it funds your CPF LIFE payouts.
ra.body:
At {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation}, CPF moves savings into a new Retirement Account: first from the Special Account, then from the Ordinary Account, until the Full Retirement Sum (FRS) for your year is reached. There are three levels — the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS), the FRS, and the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS), {policy:cpf.retirement_sums.ers_multiple} times the FRS, the most you can put in.

If you own a property with enough lease left, you can pledge it and set aside only the BRS in cash; the rest above it may be withdrawn, but the CPF LIFE payout is then lower.

Tip: CPF used for a home is not in the RA. Plan → CPF & retirement shows the RA at {policy:cpf.age.ra_formation} with and without the flat you picked, and ticks each sum met.

refinancing.short: Replacing an existing home loan with a new one, usually for a lower rate or different terms, while keeping the same flat.
refinancing.body:
Refinancing means taking a new loan to pay off the old one. Borrowers do this when another lender offers a better rate or more suitable terms. Switching to a new package with the same bank is often called repricing.

For HDB flats, a borrower can move from an HDB loan to a bank loan, but cannot move from a bank loan back to an HDB loan. That makes leaving an HDB loan a one-way step.

Costs to weigh include legal and valuation fees (sometimes subsidised by the new lender) and any penalty if the current loan is still within its lock-in period. The new loan is assessed under MAS rules, which include some relaxations for owner-occupiers refinancing their own home.

Worked example: e.g. a S$300,000 balance with 20 years left, moving from 4.2% to 3.2%, cuts the instalment from about S$1,850 to about S$1,690 a month — a saving to compare against the switching costs.

Tip: Refinancing does not change the outstanding balance; it changes the rate and terms applied to it.

remaining-lease.short: The number of years left on a flat's lease at a given date — a key driver of price, loan size and how much CPF can be used.
remaining-lease.formula: Remaining lease = lease commencement year + lease term − current year
remaining-lease.body:
Remaining lease counts down from {policy:lease.term.years} years from the lease commencement date. Two otherwise similar flats can differ by decades in remaining lease, and the difference shows up in price, financing and resale prospects.

Several rules depend on it. CPF savings can be used in full only if the remaining lease covers the youngest buyer to age {policy:cpf.lease.cover_to_age}, and not at all below {policy:cpf.lease.min_years} years. An HDB loan's tenure cannot run beyond the remaining lease minus {policy:tenure.hdb.lease_buffer} years.

Worked example: e.g. a flat whose lease began 41 years ago has the full lease term minus 41 years remaining, and that figure falls by one every year the owner lives there.

Tip: The lease that will be left when the flat is eventually sold matters as much as the lease left today.

renovation.short: Money set aside for works and furnishing after collecting the keys; it cannot come from CPF savings or the housing loan.
renovation.body:
Resale flats vary widely in condition. Some are ready to move into; others, especially older flats, may need rewiring, new plumbing, kitchen and bathroom works, or new flooring. These costs come on top of the purchase price.

Renovation is paid in cash or with a separate renovation loan; CPF savings and the housing loan cannot be used for it. HDB also sets renovation rules — some works need a permit — and contractors must be listed in HDB's Directory of Renovation Contractors.

Worked example: e.g. a household with S$40,000 in cash that needs S$25,000 for COV and fees has about S$15,000 left for renovation. That may make a well-kept flat at a slightly higher price easier to fund than a cheaper flat needing major works.

Tip: When comparing flats, the likely renovation cost belongs in the comparison alongside the price difference.

resale-levy.short: An amount you usually pay when you buy a second subsidised flat after selling your first one, so that housing subsidies are shared fairly.
resale-levy.body:
A flat bought from HDB, or a resale flat bought with a CPF housing grant, is a subsidised flat. If you sold one and then buy a second subsidised flat — a new flat from HDB or a new executive condo from a developer — you usually pay a resale levy for the second one.

The levy is a fixed amount set by the type of the first subsidised flat you sold. It is payable when you buy the second subsidised flat.

Tip: Ask HDB for the exact levy before you apply. The Plan tab shows it in the sale breakdown when you sell a subsidised flat and buy again.

rpi.short: HDB's quarterly index of overall resale flat prices, measured against a base quarter, used to track market trends over time.
rpi.formula: % change = (RPI this quarter ÷ RPI earlier quarter − 1) × 100
rpi.body:
The RPI summarises how HDB resale prices as a whole have moved over time. It is set relative to a base quarter, so a reading above the base value means prices are higher on average than in that quarter. HDB publishes a flash estimate as each quarter ends and the final figure a few weeks later.

The index accounts for differences in the mix of flats sold — such as type, location and age — so it reflects price trends better than a simple average of transaction prices.

Worked example: e.g. if the RPI rises from 180 to 189, resale prices have risen by about 5% on average over that period, though individual towns and flat types can move differently.

Tip: The RPI describes the whole market; this app's recent-sales benchmark looks at a specific block or town, which can diverge from the overall trend.

scc.short: S&CC is a monthly fee your town council charges for cleaning, lifts and upkeep of common areas — it is separate from grants and ABSD, which are about buying. Town councils set different rates by household type: the lower rate is for citizen households without private, industrial or commercial property. We use the lower rate when a buyer is a Singapore Citizen, so check your town council for the exact rate.
scc.body:
Every HDB flat owner pays service and conservancy charges to the Town Council that manages the estate. The money funds cleaning, lift maintenance, landscaping, common-area lighting, and a sinking fund for longer-term works such as repainting and re-roofing.

Charges are set by each Town Council and differ by flat type — larger flats pay more — and by town. Eligible Singaporean households receive periodic S&CC rebates from the Government, credited directly to their Town Council accounts.

Worked example: e.g. if S&CC were S$80 a month, that is S$960 a year — a small but permanent addition to housing costs.

Tip: S&CC, property tax and utilities are recurring costs of ownership that are easy to overlook when comparing a flat's instalment with rent.

shb.short: A cash bonus of up to {policy:seniors.shb.total_max} for owners aged {policy:seniors.shb.min_age} or older who sell their home, buy a smaller HDB flat and put part of the sale money into their CPF Retirement Account.
shb.body:
"Right-sizing" means moving to a smaller flat later in life. The Silver Housing Bonus rewards doing it in a way that adds to retirement income: you commit to a net increase in your Retirement Account (RA) of up to {policy:seniors.shb.full_topup} from the sale, and receive up to {policy:seniors.shb.bonus_max} for that part — plus up to {policy:seniors.shb.two_room_extra} more when the next home is a two-room Flexi flat.

At least one owner must be a Singapore Citizen aged {policy:seniors.shb.min_age} or older, household income within {policy:seniors.shb.income_ceiling} a month, and the smaller flat bought within {policy:seniors.shb.purchase_window_months} months of selling. CPF money refunded from the sale counts towards the top-up.

Tip: The Options card in Plan shows the right-sizing path with the flat you picked as the next home. CPF's page lists every condition.

single.short: An unmarried Singapore Citizen buying alone or with other singles. Singles can buy a resale flat from age {policy:eligibility.single.min_age} and a new flat only as a two-room Flexi.
single.body:
HDB treats a buyer without a spouse or family nucleus as a single. The singles scheme is for Singapore Citizens: from age {policy:eligibility.single.min_age} a single can buy a resale flat of most types, or a new 2-room Flexi flat in any location. Singles may also buy together with other singles (the Joint Singles Scheme).

Grants and the HDB loan for singles use their own income ceiling of {policy:eligibility.income_ceiling.single} a month and smaller grant amounts than families.

A single Permanent Resident cannot buy an HDB flat; renting or a private home are the routes until citizenship.

Tip: In Your household, choose "Single" under Buying as — the flat types and grants then follow the singles rules.

sora.short: Singapore's benchmark interest rate, administered by MAS, which most floating-rate bank home loans now use as their reference rate.
sora.formula: Floating loan rate = compounded SORA (e.g. 3-month) + bank spread
sora.body:
SORA is the volume-weighted average rate at which banks borrow Singapore dollars from each other overnight, without collateral. MAS calculates and publishes it every business day. It replaced older benchmarks such as SIBOR and SOR for Singapore-dollar loans.

Floating-rate home loans usually quote a compounded SORA average over a past period — such as one or three months — plus a fixed spread set by the bank. When SORA moves, the loan rate and therefore the instalment move with it at the next reset.

Worked example: e.g. if compounded SORA is 2.0% and the spread is 0.8%, the loan rate is 2.8%; if SORA later rises to 3.0%, the rate becomes 3.8%.

Tip: SORA can move a lot within a few years. The HDB concessionary loan rate is not linked to SORA; it follows the CPF Ordinary Account rate.

stress-test.short: Checking whether the instalment would still be affordable if interest rates were higher than today — the idea behind the floor rates lenders apply.
stress-test.formula: Stressed instalment = instalment recomputed at (current rate + rate shock)
stress-test.body:
A stress test asks "what if rates go up?". Regulators build one into every loan approval through floor rates: {policy:rate.floor.hdb} for HDB loans and {policy:rate.floor.bank} for bank loans. The instalment at that rate must fit within the MSR cap of {policy:ratio.msr.cap} of income.

Households can run their own stress test too, by recomputing the instalment at a higher rate and comparing it with take-home pay, not just gross income. This is most relevant for floating-rate loans, whose instalments change as benchmarks move.

Worked example: e.g. a S$400,000 loan over 20 years: at 3.2% the instalment is about S$2,260; adding a shock of 1.5 percentage points (to 4.7%) raises it to about S$2,570.

Tip: Income can be stress-tested as well — a period of lower income, such as during a job change or parental leave, raises the share of income going to the loan.

tdsr.short: For bank loans, the cap on all monthly debt repayments together — home loan, car loan, card minimums and others — at {policy:ratio.tdsr.cap} of gross monthly income.
tdsr.formula: TDSR = all monthly debt repayments (incl. the new instalment) ÷ gross monthly income
tdsr.body:
TDSR looks at every debt a borrower is servicing, not just the new home loan. Car loans, other property loans, personal and study loans, and credit-card minimum payments all count. MAS caps the total at {policy:ratio.tdsr.cap} of gross monthly income for property loans from banks and financial institutions. HDB loans are assessed on MSR instead.

For an HDB flat bought with a bank loan, both limits apply: the home-loan instalment must stay within the MSR cap of {policy:ratio.msr.cap}, and all debts together within TDSR. As with MSR, the new mortgage is assessed at the higher of the actual rate and the bank floor rate of {policy:rate.floor.bank}.

Worked example: e.g. a buyer earning S$6,000 a month with a S$700 car instalment. The car loan uses up part of the TDSR room, so less is left for the mortgage, even though the MSR test on its own is unaffected.

Tip: Being a guarantor for someone else's loan can also count towards TDSR, so listing every commitment early avoids surprises at loan approval.

tenure.short: The number of years over which a home loan is repaid; a longer tenure lowers the monthly instalment but raises the total interest paid.
tenure.body:
Tenure is how long the loan runs. For an HDB loan it is the shortest of {policy:tenure.hdb.max} years, age {policy:tenure.age_cap} minus the buyers' average age, and the remaining lease minus {policy:tenure.hdb.lease_buffer} years. For a bank loan on an HDB flat the cap is {policy:tenure.bank.hdb_flat.max} years, but going beyond {policy:loan.bank.hdb_flat.full_ltv_max_tenure} years, or past age {policy:tenure.age_cap}, cuts the LTV to {policy:loan.bank.ltv.lower_tier}.

A longer tenure spreads the repayments over more months, so each instalment is smaller and the MSR test is easier to pass. The trade-off is that interest is paid for longer, so the total interest is higher.

Worked example: e.g. a S$400,000 loan at an illustrative 3.2% costs about S$2,260 a month over 20 years but about S$1,730 over 30 years — while total interest rises from about S$142,000 to about S$223,000.

Tip: Older buyers often get a shorter tenure because of the age limit, which raises the instalment for the same loan.

total-interest.short: The sum of all interest paid over the life of a loan — all instalments added up, minus the amount originally borrowed.
total-interest.formula: Total interest = instalment × number of months − loan amount
total-interest.body:
Total interest is the price of borrowing. It depends on the loan size, the rate and, very strongly, the tenure: stretching the loan over more years lowers the instalment but means paying interest for longer.

Worked example: e.g. a S$400,000 loan at an illustrative 3.2%. Over 20 years the instalment is about S$2,260 and total interest about S$142,000; over 30 years the instalment drops to about S$1,730, but total interest rises to about S$223,000.

Total interest on the loan is separate from the cost of using CPF. CPF savings used for the flat also build up accrued interest, which must be refunded to the owners' CPF accounts when the flat is sold.

Tip: Looking at total interest alongside the monthly instalment shows the full trade-off between tenures, not just the monthly one.

upfront-cost.short: All the money needed at or before completion — downpayment, any COV, stamp duties and fees — as distinct from the monthly instalments afterwards.
upfront-cost.formula: Upfront = downpayment + COV + BSD + ABSD + legal and other fees
upfront-cost.body:
Affordability has two sides: can the household keep up with the monthly instalment, and can it fund the purchase in the first place? Upfront cost answers the second question.

It typically includes the downpayment, any Cash Over Valuation, Buyer's Stamp Duty, Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty if it applies, the option and exercise fees (which count towards the price), legal and conveyancing fees, and valuation fees. Renovation and furnishing usually follow soon after.

Some items can be paid from CPF Ordinary Account savings; others must be cash — COV always, and with a bank loan at least {policy:downpayment.bank.cash_min} of the price. Housing grants credited to CPF reduce the total.

Worked example: e.g. a S$600,000 flat bought with S$15,000 COV: the cash needed includes that S$15,000 plus any cash part of the downpayment, while stamp duty and legal fees might come from CPF.

Tip: The split between cash and CPF matters as much as the total, because cash is often the tighter constraint.

valuation.short: HDB's assessment of a resale flat's market value, requested after the Option to Purchase is granted; it caps the loan and CPF usage.
valuation.formula: Loan and CPF base = lower of (agreed price, HDB valuation)
valuation.body:
Buyers paying with CPF savings or a housing loan must submit a Request for Value to HDB once they hold an Option to Purchase. HDB then assesses the flat, and the result becomes the reference for the maximum loan — {policy:loan.hdb.ltv} for an HDB loan or {policy:loan.bank.ltv} for a bank loan — and for how much CPF can be used.

The valuation is independent of the agreed price. If the price is above it, the gap is Cash Over Valuation, payable in cash. If the price is at or below the valuation, the loan and CPF limits are based on the price instead.

Worked example: e.g. agreed price S$580,000, valuation S$590,000: the loan is based on S$580,000, the lower figure, and there is no COV.

Tip: The valuation result is valid only for a limited period, so the resale application has to follow within that window, or a new request is needed.

vl-wl.short: Caps on CPF use for a home — the Valuation Limit is the lower of price and valuation; with a bank loan, the Withdrawal Limit is {policy:proposed.cpf.wl.multiple_of_vl} of it.
vl-wl.formula: VL = lower of (price, valuation); WL = VL × WL multiple
vl-wl.body:
The Valuation Limit (VL) is the lower of the purchase price and the flat's value at the time of purchase. CPF Ordinary Account savings can be used for the downpayment and instalments until the total CPF used reaches the VL.

Beyond the VL, members can continue using OA savings only after setting aside the Basic Retirement Sum in CPF. For an HDB flat with an HDB loan, the reference point is the VL itself. With a bank loan, continued use is capped at the Withdrawal Limit (WL) of {policy:proposed.cpf.wl.multiple_of_vl} of the VL. Once a limit is reached and the conditions are not met, instalments must be paid in cash.

Worked example: e.g. a flat bought at S$600,000 and valued at S$590,000 has a VL of S$590,000. CPF used across all owners counts towards it, including the downpayment and every instalment paid from CPF.

Tip: These limits mainly bite late in a long loan, when years of CPF-funded instalments have added up.
